why_how.text: After involvement in a crash, stop at once in a safe location.
The handbook requires immediate notice to the nearest law-enforcement agency when a crash causes injury or death, or property damage exceeding five hundred dollars.
Provide reasonable assistance to an injured person after a crash.
Warn approaching traffic only when doing so does not put you or others at risk; use hazard lamps if possible and reflective triangles when available.
Exchange the driver's name, address, plate number and license number with others involved in the crash, and obtain the corresponding information from the other driver.
If you damage a vehicle with nobody attending it, locate its owner or leave a note where that owner can readily find it. Include your contact name and address plus the name of your vehicle's owner.
Do not assume someone is uninjured merely because the person says so; seek professional assistance promptly.

why_how.text: Avoid unnecessary movement of an injured person, since unskilled handling may worsen an injury.

After a crash on a multilane highway or expressway with no apparent serious injury or death, drivers must move the involved vehicles to a safe refuge when the vehicles can be driven normally and safely.
Move a crash vehicle only if doing so will not create further danger or harm to people, the vehicles or the roadway.
If a crash participant cannot move the vehicle, that person may ask a nearby driver with a valid license of the appropriate class to move it.
Moving a vehicle to safety under the described crash rule does not by itself establish fault or eliminate the driver's duties to stop and provide information.
A driver who moves a crash vehicle under the safety rule retains the ability to file a written report with the local police agency.

why_how.text: Deer behavior is unpredictable; an animal standing beside the road may run toward traffic when startled rather than away from it.
In areas known for deer, continually scan both the traveled road and its shoulders for animals.
Slow when a deer crosses ahead of your vehicle or another vehicle, since deer often travel in groups and another may follow.
If a deer is seen beside or on the road at night, reduce speed immediately and use low beams to avoid dazzling it.
When an animal runs into the path, reduce speed as much as possible. The handbook warns against swerving for a deer because that can cause a collision with traffic or a departure from the roadway.
After a collision involving a deer, notify the police as soon as possible.
Be especially alert for roadside deer in early morning and late evening, while remembering that deer can also appear at other times of day.
